en: Narra, the national tree, produces dense, termite-resistant wood because its heartwood contains high levels of natural protective oils.
The national flower, Sampaguita, releases its strongest sweet scent at night to attract nocturnal moth pollinators.
The national animal, the carabao, wallows in mud to cool down because it lacks sufficient sweat glands.
The Ifugao rice terraces use muyong, an indigenous science where forested mountain catchments naturally filter and channel rainwater downward.
Artisans weave Barong Tagalog from piña fibers, which are mechanically scraped from the leaves of the Red Spanish pineapple.
The national gem, the golden pearl, forms inside large pearl oysters when they secrete nacre around an irritant.
T'boli weavers create T'nalak cloth from abaca, a native banana plant whose fibers become stronger when air-dried.
The national fruit, the Carabao mango, turns yellow when ethylene gas breaks down its green chlorophyll during ripening.
Mayon Volcano’s perfect cone shape results from alternating layers of hardened lava and volcanic ash from repeated eruptions.
National Scientist Dr. Ramon Barba discovered that spraying potassium nitrate on mango trees induces flowering during the dry season.
The traditional salakot hat is woven from rattan, a climbing palm whose solid outer skin provides lightweight sunshade.
Farmers cultivate the national fish, bangus, in coastal pens because mangrove estuaries provide a nutrient-rich nursery environment.
